For people who know they are wrong more often than they would like

Calibrate what you predict about yourself

The problem: your expectation and your reality do not match. The gap hurts or confuses. The ESTIMAT app may help you negotiate it.

With the ESTIMAT app we seek your long-term wellbeing. We propose a path: knowing yourself with your own data, in what goes well and in what goes badly. You see where your predictions about yourself fail and you decide better with that. That it works is a bet, and we invite you to make it with us. It may help you a lot or a little. In the end you will have data to judge how much knowing yourself is worth in your life.

Biases

Which errors we want to shrink

Six known errors in predicting about yourself. For each, how the app may help. That the app reduces them is our hypothesis, not a finding.

1/6 · Hedonic adaptation

You get used to what you achieved and it stops counting. You see what is missing, not what you already did.

How the ESTIMAT app may help: Home puts your accumulated satisfaction at the center: everything you got, not just today.

Frederick and Loewenstein, 1999.
2/6 · Planning fallacy

You underestimate the time and effort of your tasks, even when it has happened before.

How the ESTIMAT app may help: You predict energy before acting and compare afterwards. You see your error by area.

Buehler, Griffin and Ross, 1994.
3/6 · Affective forecasting error

You overestimate how much something will satisfy you, or how much it will hurt.

How the ESTIMAT app may help: You predict satisfaction. In Return, you log the real one.

Wilson and Gilbert, 2005.
4/6 · Emotion of the moment

What you feel now colors what you expect from the future.

How the ESTIMAT app may help: You name the emotion before predicting. The app shows your error by emotion.

Lerner and Keltner, 2001.
5/6 · Hindsight bias

Once you know the outcome, you think you saw it coming.

How the ESTIMAT app may help: Your prediction is saved with a date before you act. You compare against what you wrote, not what you remember.

Fischhoff, 1975.
6/6 · Overconfidence

Your certainty runs ahead of your hits.

How the ESTIMAT app may help: You mark how confident you are in each prediction. Then you compare it with what happened.

Lichtenstein, Fischhoff and Phillips, 1982.
The app

How it works

We map expectations, invest in actions and compare the return. Each turn gives you a new data point on how you predict.

Start with one part

You do not have to log everything. You can start with one task you want to improve, or with a return per period: the day, the week or the month. The full map and the other functions open when you want. Our bet is that going step by step helps you keep it up.

Screens show sample data. The app is in Spanish and Portuguese.

Let’s bet together: the more you know yourself, the more you flow.

Extra: emotions

Know yourself through the history of your emotions

Affect: what you feel, named or not. A map to learn, bit by bit, what each emotion is for. It starts from Robert Kurzban’s evolutionary theory. The order and the links are our proposal. Many emotions are old and hard to change. The bet is to use them better, from their function. Below, three published results and one hypothesis of ours, kept apart so they do not blur.

Lab finding

Naming lowers the alarm

Lieberman and colleagues showed emotional faces to people in a scanner. When participants picked the word for the emotion, the amygdala responded less than in other tasks with the same face. Right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex was more active.

Lieberman et al., 2007. Limit: brief stimuli, in the lab.
Review

Distinguishing more specific emotions helps regulation

People who tell their negative emotions apart more finely turn less to harmful strategies, such as binge drinking or aggression. A review by Kashdan, Barrett and McKnight sums this up.

Kashdan et al., 2015. Limit: largely correlational.
Experiment

Emotion changes what you predict

Fearful people estimate more risk. Angry people estimate less. The emotion of the moment changes what you think will happen.

Lerner and Keltner, 2001.
Our hypothesis, untested

Naming and comparing calibrates

If you name what you feel precisely and then compare prediction with outcome, your error shrinks over time. The ESTIMAT app exists to measure that with your own data.

It may be false. Below we say how we would know.

For the skeptic

What we claim and what we do not

error = prediction − outcome · by action, by area and by emotion

We claim

  • The app measures your prediction error from your own records.
  • It stores your confidence in each prediction, so you can check it against your hits.
  • The emotion map adapts Robert Kurzban’s taxonomy (2025). His four kingdoms are our four levels.
  • Your data stays on your device. No account. You can export a copy.

We do not claim

  • That the effect is shown. So far, one person uses it daily.
  • That each emotion’s function is proven. They are evolutionary hypotheses.
  • That it replaces therapy. It does not.
  • That our adaptation is Kurzban’s. We placed some emotions by our own judgment.

Three hypotheses your data can refute

Precision and calibrationPeople who name their affect in more detail reduce their error over the following weeks more than those who only mark pleasant or unpleasant.
Mood and biasAffect at the start predicts the direction of the error: a pleasant mood tends toward overestimating, an unpleasant one toward underestimating.
Levels and returnActions aimed at more integrating levels yield more satisfaction per hour, with more variance.

If any of them fails on real data, we change it. Tell us which one looks weakest.

Why it exists

Being wrong less, at the root

I am looking for ways to be wrong less, and not bit by bit: at the root. I tried many apps and models. There is a lot that is good and a lot that promises much, but they lacked a line tying the concepts together.

The ESTIMAT app is my attempt to tie them together. From systems theory it takes a way to split what I want into parts. From cybernetics, the loop that measures how wrong I am and tries to correct it.

This way emotion stops being noise. It becomes data I can calibrate.

What matters most to me comes next. I want to bring a lighter version, with a narrator telling a story, to teenagers and children in neighborhoods where crime comes looking for them early. I believe self-knowledge is where we can act the most. It is a bet, and I will measure it the way I measure everything else.

The creator of the ESTIMAT app, a neuroscientist in Argentina. He works with incarcerated people and with an NGO in Brazil.
My data, n = 1
